The concept of waste heat being beneficial is a red herring for a large part. A 60W bulb generates 3.3 BTU of heat per watt or ~200 BTU total. The best generators are 25% - 30% efficient so your 60 watt bulb requires 600 BTU worth of diesel fuel to power. A 60 watt equivalent LED uses 10 watts/33 BTU total so requires ~100 Diesel BTU's to generate. A decent diesel stove is 80+% efficient making it the az heat source of choice. Moreover, LED's by dint of less demand allow a smaller generating capacity or allow for an entire engine to be shut down if the efficiencies in a community are scaled. They also have proportionally less line loss from generator to bulb, aka distribution loss. We were able to downsize a cabin from a 2kw Honda to a 1kw unit by converting first to CFL's then LED's with the bonus of being able to run an electric coffee pot with a few lights!

Further, the demographics of the CR subscriber base are, in general, the type that would buy a Toyota (risk averse) and demonstrate confirmation bias for their choices.  Thus the traditional Japanese brands skew favourably and most other brands go the opposite direction.

Is CR a useful tool as part of overall vehicle shopping?  Yes, but it should be considered as only 1 piece of data (opinion) as it lacks objectivity and scientific rigour.

Orcas are *extremely* familial.. They live in matriarchal pods, which are essentially extended families. Typically several pods will live somewhat close together, and females from one pod will mate with males from another. Prior to becoming a mother herself, which usually starts at around 10-12 years old (IIRC.) a female orca will stay with her mother and siblings. Once a female has her first calf, her mother will help teach her how to care for it. After that, she may spend less time with her mother and siblings, but she'll almost always remain part of the same pod. Male orcas generally stay at their mother's side until one of them passes away. They tend not to be very involved with their own offspring, but they help their mothers (and sometimes sisters) raise future calves, allowing the females to focus on the youngest ones who need the most attention or one who has just had her first calf.  The social and family structures of orcas are just fascinating.
